15: # Command Creation - Argument Hints and Modes
16: 
17: Depth for SKILL.md Steps 6 and 10: the surface where a command declares its inputs. Use these patterns when writing `argument-hint`, choosing `:auto`/`:confirm` behavior, or tightening frontmatter.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: This reference collects the input-declaration patterns that would bloat the SKILL.md workflow: a catalog of `argument-hint` shapes, the design intent behind `:auto`/`:confirm` modes, and budget-minded frontmatter tips for `description` and `allowed-tools`.
24: 
25: ---
26: 
27: ## 2. ARGUMENT-HINT DESIGN PATTERNS
28: 
29: Use `argument-hint` when the command expects user input. Required arguments use angle brackets. Optional arguments use square brackets. Mode suffixes such as `[:auto|:confirm]` are optional selectors, not required content.
30: 
31: | Pattern | Example | Use When |
32: |---|---|---|
33: | Required subject | `"<spec-folder>"` | The command cannot run without one primary input |
34: | Required plus optional mode | `"<request> [:auto|:confirm]"` | Mode selection changes execution pace |
35: | Optional action or query | `"[action|query] [options]"` | Empty input can show help or use a safe default |
36: | Required target plus flags | `"<path> [--dry-run] [--confirm]"` | Flags alter safety or preview behavior |
37: | Namespace operation | `"<skill-name> [--validate]"` | The namespace/action is in the invocation path, not the hint |
38: 
39: **Good hints**:
40: - `"<task> [:auto|:confirm]"`
41: - `"<spec-folder> [--strict]"`
42: - `"[status|repair|validate] [target]"`
43: 
44: **Weak hints**:
45: - `"args"` because it does not tell the user what to provide
46: - `"<optional-target>"` because required syntax contradicts the word optional
47: - `"<query> [query]"` because it duplicates the same concept in two forms
48: 
49: Mandatory-gate reminder: when the hint contains any required `<argument>`, the command needs a blocking input gate after the H1 and its purpose line, before any workflow step. The gate must ignore mode suffixes when deciding whether real required content exists.
50: 
51: ---
52: 
53: ## 3. `:auto` VS `:confirm` MODE DESIGN
54: 
55: Use modes when the same workflow needs different execution pacing.
56: 
57: | Mode | Design Intent | Good Fit |
58: |---|---|---|
59: | `:auto` | Execute without approval gates, self-validating at checkpoints | Low-risk repeatable workflows with clear defaults |
60: | `:confirm` | Pause after steps for user approval, modification, skip, or abort | Workflows with ambiguity, review checkpoints, or higher risk |
61: | no suffix | Ask the user to choose mode | Commands where neither pace is universally safe |
62: 
63: `:auto` should still stop when required input is missing, destructive impact is unclear, or a default would be fabricated. Autonomous does not mean permission to invent.
64: 
65: `:confirm` should not ask tiny repetitive questions. Batch setup into one consolidated prompt, then pause at meaningful checkpoints.
66: 
67: If a command combines modes with argument dispatch, parse mode first and dispatch the remaining arguments after removing the suffix.
68: 
69: ---
70: 
71: ## 4. FRONTMATTER AND DESCRIPTION BUDGET TIPS
72: 
73: Every command needs YAML frontmatter with a single-line `description`. Add `argument-hint` and `allowed-tools` when applicable.
74: 
75: ```yaml
76: ---
77: description: Review a spec packet with :auto or :confirm execution
78: argument-hint: "<spec-folder> [:auto|:confirm]"
79: allowed-tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, Task
80: ---
81: ```
82: 
83: **Description tips**:
84: - start with an action verb when possible
85: - keep it concise and single-line
86: - target 110 characters or less
87: - retain important trigger tokens such as `:auto` and `:confirm` when they are part of the command contract
88: - do not use YAML block scalars for `description`
89: - avoid product lists or implementation detail that belongs in the body
90: 
91: **Allowed-tools tips**:
92: - list only tools the command actually uses
93: - do not add broad tools just in case
94: - use fully qualified MCP IDs in `allowed-tools`, such as `mcp__<server>__<tool>`
95: - use bare MCP tool names only in prose, not in frontmatter
96: 
97: ---
98: 
99: ## 5. RELATED RESOURCES
100: 
101: - [README.md](README.md) - command-creation reference map
102: - [worked-example.md](worked-example.md) - frontmatter and gate applied in a full command
103: - [common-pitfalls.md](common-pitfalls.md) - hint, mode, and frontmatter mistakes with fixes

13: 
14: # Command Template - OpenCode Slash Commands
15: 
16: Templates for creating slash commands with proper frontmatter, mandatory gates, and structured workflows.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### What Are OpenCode Commands?
23: 
24: **OpenCode commands** are slash-triggered instructions (e.g., `/speckit:complete`, `/speckit:save`) that automate workflows, enforce patterns, and extend AI agent capabilities. They're markdown files that define structured behavior for specific tasks.
25: 
26: **Core Purpose**:
27: - **Workflow automation** - Multi-step processes become single invocations
28: - **Pattern enforcement** - Consistent behavior across sessions
29: - **Task routing** - Arguments dispatch to appropriate handlers
30: - **User guidance** - Structured prompts prevent errors
31: - **Tool restriction** - Limit which tools the command can use
32: 
33: **Key Difference from Skills**:
34: - Commands = Actionable workflows triggered by `/command-name`
35: - Skills = Reference documentation loaded via `Read(".skilled/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md")`
36: 
37: ### Core Characteristics
38: 
39: | Characteristic         | Description                                           |
40: | ---------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
41: | **Markdown-based**     | Human-readable instruction files                      |
42: | **Frontmatter-driven** | Metadata controls behavior (description, args, tools) |
43: | **Argument-aware**     | Parse and validate user input via `$ARGUMENTS`        |
44: | **Status-reporting**   | Return structured outcomes (`STATUS=OK\|FAIL`)        |
45: | **Tool-restricted**    | `allowed-tools` limits available tools                |
46: 
47: ### How Commands Are Invoked
48: 
49: ```
50: User types: /command-name arguments
51:                 │           │
52:                 │           └─► Passed as $ARGUMENTS variable
53:                 │
54:                 └─► OpenCode finds .opencode/commands/command-name.md
55:                     │
56:                     ├─► Loads frontmatter (description, tools, hints)
57:                     │
58:                     ├─► Injects $ARGUMENTS into instruction body
59:                     │
60:                     └─► AI agent executes instructions step-by-step
61: ```
62: 
63: > **Description budget**: command `description:` fields share the Claude Code skill-metadata budget (default 8,000 chars total). Keep each command description **≤ 110 chars**, retain `:auto`/`:confirm` mode suffixes (advisor trigger tokens), no product enumerations. See [`assets/frontmatter-templates.md` § Description Budget & Trim Style](../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for the canonical trim rules.
64: 
65: ### Command File Location
66: 
67: ```
68: .skilled/
69: └── command/
70:     ├── simple-command.md          → /simple-command
71:     ├── workflow-command.md        → /workflow-command
72:     └── namespace/                  → Grouped commands
73:         ├── action1.md             → /namespace:action1
74:         └── action2.md             → /namespace:action2
75: ```
76: 
77: ### Progressive Complexity
78: 
79: ```
80: Level 1: Simple Command
81:          └─ Single action, few arguments (~50-100 lines)
82:             ↓
83: Level 2: Workflow Command
84:          └─ Multi-step process with validation (~100-200 lines)
85:             ↓
86: Level 3: Mode-Based / Dispatch Command
87:          └─ Complex routing, user control (~150-300 lines)
88: ```
89:

92: ## 2. WHEN TO CREATE COMMANDS
93: 
94: ### Create Command When
95: 
96: - Multi-step process with defined phases
97: - Repeated task needing consistency across sessions
98: - Requires confirmation gates (destructive actions)
99: - Multiple argument patterns need routing
100: - User should control execution pace (`:auto`/`:confirm` modes)
101: - Tool restrictions needed for security/focus
102: 
103: ### Use Skill Instead When
104: 
105: - Content is reference material, not executable workflow
106: - Complex domain knowledge that multiple commands might need
107: - Reusable patterns/standards across multiple commands
108: 
109: ### Decision Framework
110: 
111: ```
112: Is this a repeatable workflow with defined steps?
113: ├─► YES
114: │   │
115: │   ├─► Does it need user arguments?
116: │   │   └─► Command with argument-hint + mandatory gate
117: │   │
118: │   ├─► Does it have modes (auto/confirm)?
119: │   │   └─► Mode-based command template
120: │   │
121: │   ├─► Is it destructive/irreversible?
122: │   │   └─► Destructive command template
123: │   │
124: │   ├─► Multiple action keywords (start/stop/status)?
125: │   │   └─► Argument dispatch pattern
126: │   │
127: │   └─► Simple single action?
128: │       └─► Simple command template
129: │
130: └─► NO
131:     │
132:     ├─► Is it reference documentation?
133:     │   └─► Create Skill instead
134:     │
135:     ├─► Is it reusable knowledge?
136:     │   └─► Create Skill instead
137:     │
138:     └─► Is it one-time task?
139:         └─► Just do it (no command needed)
140: ```
141: 
142: ### Command Types by Complexity
143: 
144: | Type                  | Complexity | Lines       | Use When                                 |
145: | --------------------- | ---------- | ----------- | ---------------------------------------- |
146: | **Simple**            | Low        | 50-100      | Single action, few args                  |
147: | **Workflow**          | Medium     | 100-200     | Multi-step process with outputs          |
148: | **Mode-Based**        | Medium     | 150-250     | User controls execution pace             |
149: | **Argument Dispatch** | Medium     | 150-300     | Multiple entry points/actions            |
150: | **Destructive**       | Medium     | 100-180     | Irreversible actions, needs confirmation |
151: | **Namespace**         | Varies     | 50-150 each | Related commands grouped together        |

194: ## 4. STANDARD COMMAND STRUCTURE
195: 
196: ### Common Sections (All Command Types)
197: 
198: | Order | Section             | Required         | Purpose                             |
199: | ----- | ------------------- | ---------------- | ----------------------------------- |
200: | 0     | **Frontmatter**     | Yes              | Metadata (description, args, tools) |
201: | 1     | **Mandatory Gate**  | If required args | Prevent context inference           |
202: | 2     | **Title + Purpose** | Yes              | What the command does               |
203: | 3     | **Contract**        | Recommended      | Inputs/outputs specification        |
204: | 4     | **Instructions**    | Yes              | Step-by-step execution              |
205: | 5     | **Examples**        | Recommended      | Usage demonstrations                |
206: | 6     | **Notes**           | Optional         | Caveats, requirements               |
207: 
208: > **Frontmatter budget:** keep `argument-hint` at or under 140 characters. It **summarizes** the invocation shape while the router's **EXECUTION TARGETS** section **enumerates** the full flag surface. Over-budget hints warn, they never block registration.
209: 
210: ### Minimal Command Structure
211: 
212: ```markdown
213: ---
214: description: [Action verb] [what it does]
215: argument-hint: "<required> [optional]"
216: allowed-tools: Tool1, Tool2
217: ---
218: 
219: # Command Title
220: 
221: [One sentence describing purpose.]
222: 
223: <!-- REQUIRED-ARGUMENT GATE: keep this block whenever argument-hint declares a required
224: <argument>. Delete it only for a command that takes none. It is the reason a command stops
225: instead of inventing an input from context. -->
226: 
227: ### MANDATORY INPUT GATE
228: 
229: **STATUS: BLOCKED** until `<required>` is bound.
230: 
231: 1. Parse `$ARGUMENTS`, stripping any mode suffix and flags before resolving the required input.
232: 2. Treat an absent or whitespace-only value as missing. Do not infer it from conversation
233:    history, open files, screenshots, or repository state.
234: 3. When it is missing, ask for it with clear options or an expected reply format, stop, and
235:    wait. Use only `$ARGUMENTS` or that explicit reply.
236: 
237: ## 1. PURPOSE
238: 
239: [2-3 sentences explaining the command.]
240: 
241: ## 2. INSTRUCTIONS
242: 
243: ### Step 1: [Name]
244: [Instructions]
245: 
246: ### Step 2: Return Status
247: - Success: `STATUS=OK`
248: - Failure: `STATUS=FAIL ERROR="<message>"`
249: ```
250:

252: 
253: ## 5. STEP NUMBERING RULES
254: 
255: **Rule**: Use full integers only (1, 2, 3). No decimals (1.5, 2.5) or sub-steps (1.1, 1.2).
256: 
257: | Element  | Correct                   | Wrong              |
258: | -------- | ------------------------- | ------------------ |
259: | Steps    | Step 1, Step 2, Step 3    | Step 1.5, Step 2.5 |
260: | Phases   | PHASE 1, PHASE 2, PHASE 3 | PHASE 1.5, PHASE 2 |
261: | Sections | ## 1. PURPOSE               | ## 1.1 PURPOSE     |
262: 
263: **Sub-activities**: Use bullets within a step, not decimal sub-steps:
264: ```markdown
265: Step 3: Execute workflow
266:   - Load configuration
267:   - Validate inputs  
268:   - Run process
269: ```
270: 
271: ---
272: 
273: ## 6. SECTION VOCABULARY
274: 
275: Commands use two categories of notation: **semantic markers** (for blocking/validation states) and **section names** (for content organization).
276: 
277: ### Semantic Markers (Blocking/Validation)
278: 
279: These markers indicate workflow state and enforcement:
280: 
281: | Marker | Name    | Purpose                     | Example Usage               |
282: | ------ | ------- | --------------------------- | --------------------------- |
283: | MANDATORY | Alert   | Critical/mandatory sections | `# MANDATORY PHASES`      |
284: | PHASE  | Lock    | Phase/gate headers          | `## PHASE 1: INPUT`       |
285: | PASSED | Check   | Passed/success status       | `PASSED`                   |
286: | N/A    | Skip    | N/A or skipped              | `N/A (no memory files)`    |
287: | STOP   | Stop    | Hard stop/blocking error    | `STOP - Phase incomplete`  |
288: | WARNING| Warning | Non-blocking alert          | `VIOLATION DETECTED`       |
289: | FAILED | Fail    | Validation failure          | `FAILED`                   |
290: 
291: ### Standard Section Names
292: 
293: These names identify section types. Use EXACTLY as shown:
294: 
295: | Section      | H2 Format                    | Purpose                      |
296: | ------------ | ---------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
297: | PURPOSE      | `## N. PURPOSE`              | What the command does        |
298: | CONTRACT     | `## N. CONTRACT`             | Inputs/outputs specification |
299: | WORKFLOW     | `## N. WORKFLOW OVERVIEW`    | Process flow/steps table     |
300: | INSTRUCTIONS | `## N. INSTRUCTIONS`         | How to execute               |
301: | REFERENCE    | `## N. REFERENCE`            | Related resources            |
302: | EXAMPLES     | `## N. EXAMPLES`             | Usage demonstrations         |
303: | RELATED      | `## N. RELATED COMMANDS`     | Links to related commands    |
304: | TOOLS        | `## N. TOOL SIGNATURES`      | MCP/tool configuration       |
305: | ROUTING      | `## N. ARGUMENT ROUTING`     | Mode detection/dispatch      |
306: | DOCS         | `## N. FULL DOCUMENTATION`   | Link to full docs            |
307: | INPUT        | `## N. USER INPUT`           | User input display           |
308: 
309: ### Section Naming Rules
310: 
311: 1. **One name per purpose**: Don't reuse section names across different purposes
312: 2. **Consistent naming**: Use the same section name for the same purpose across commands
313: 3. **Exact format**: `## N. SECTION-NAME` (number, period, space, name in ALL CAPS)
314:

317: ## 7. FRONTMATTER REFERENCE
318: 
319: ### Required Fields
320: 
321: ```yaml
322: ---
323: description: Clear, action-oriented single-line description shown in /help output. Start with action verb (Create, Search, Delete, Start, Stop).
324: ---
325: ```
326: 
327: > **Important:** The `description` field MUST be a single-line string, not a YAML block scalar (`|` or `>`). Multi-line descriptions break `/help` output rendering.
328: 
329: ### Recommended Fields
330: 
331: ```yaml
332: ---
333: argument-hint: "<required> [optional] [--flag]"
334: # Format conventions:
335: #   <angle-brackets> = required argument
336: #   [square-brackets] = optional argument
337: #   --flag = boolean flag
338: #   [default: value] = argument with default
339: 
340: allowed-tools: Tool1, Tool2, Tool3
341: # Common tools: Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob, Task
342: # MCP tools: mcp__[server-name]__[tool_function]
343: ---
344: ```
345: 
346: ### Optional Fields
347: 
348: ```yaml
349: ---
350: name: command-name
351: # Override inferred name from filename
352: 
353: model: opus
354: # Override default model (USE SPARINGLY - only for complex reasoning)
355: 
356: version: 1.0.0
357: # Track command version
358: 
359: disable-model-invocation: true
360: # Prevent the AI agent from invoking this command
361: ---
362: ```
363: 
364: ### Example
365: 
366: ```yaml
367: ---
368: description: Complete spec folder workflow (5 steps) - research through implementation
369: argument-hint: "<task> [:auto|:confirm]"
370: allowed-tools: Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Task
371: ---
372: ```

376: ## 8. MANDATORY GATE PATTERN (CRITICAL)
377: 
378: ### Why This Pattern Exists
379: 
380: Without this gate, AI agents may:
381: - Infer tasks from conversation history or open files
382: - Assume what the user wants based on screenshots or context
383: - Proceed with incorrect assumptions instead of asking
384: 
385: ### When to Use
386: 
387: | Argument Type                  | Use Mandatory Gate? | Example                              |
388: | ------------------------------ | ------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
389: | `<required>` (angle brackets)  | **YES**             | `<task>`, `<query>`, `<spec-folder>` |
390: | `[optional]` (square brackets) | No (has default)    | `[count]`, `[--flag]`                |
391: | `[:auto\|:confirm]` mode flags | No (mode selection) | Mode suffixes only                   |
392: 
393: ### The Pattern
394: 
395: Add this block **after the H1 and its purpose line, before any workflow step**:
396: 
397: ```markdown
398: ### 🚨 MANDATORY FIRST ACTION - DO NOT SKIP
399: 
400: **BEFORE ANY WORKFLOW STEP, CHECK `$ARGUMENTS`:**
401: 
402: \`\`\`
403: IF $ARGUMENTS is empty, undefined, or contains only whitespace (ignoring mode flags):
404:     → STOP IMMEDIATELY
405:     → Present the user with this question:
406:         question: "[Context-appropriate question]"
407:         options:
408:           - label: "[Action label]"
409:             description: "[What user will provide]"
410:     → WAIT for user response
411:     → Use their response as the [input type]
412:     → Only THEN continue with this workflow
413: 
414: IF $ARGUMENTS contains [expected input]:
415:     → Continue reading this file
416: \`\`\`
417: 
418: **CRITICAL RULES:**
419: - **DO NOT** infer [input type] from context, screenshots, or existing files
420: - **DO NOT** assume what the user wants based on conversation history
421: - **DO NOT** proceed past this point without an explicit [input] from the user
422: - The [input] MUST come from `$ARGUMENTS` or user's answer to the question above
423: ```
424: 
425: ### Example Questions by Command Type
426: 
427: | Command Purpose    | Question                                          |
428: | ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------- |
429: | Planning           | "What would you like to plan?"                    |
430: | Research           | "What topic would you like to research?"          |
431: | Implementation     | "Which spec folder would you like to implement?"  |
432: | File improvement   | "What would you like to improve and which files?" |
433: | Prompt enhancement | "What prompt would you like to improve?"          |
434: | Generic routing    | "What request would you like to route?"           |
435: 
436: ### Multi-Phase Blocking Pattern
437: 
438: For commands requiring multiple inputs before workflow execution:
439: 
440: ```markdown
441: # 🚨 MANDATORY PHASES - BLOCKING ENFORCEMENT
442: 
443: > **HARD BLOCK**: Do not proceed past this section until ALL phases complete.
444: 
445: ## PHASE 1: INPUT COLLECTION
446: [Collect required inputs from $ARGUMENTS or prompt user]
447: 
448: ## PHASE 2: CONTEXT VERIFICATION
449: [Verify prerequisites exist]
450: 
451: ## PHASE STATUS VERIFICATION (BLOCKING)
452: 
453: | Phase            | Status | Blocker? |
454: | ---------------- | ------ | -------- |
455: | Input Collection | ✅/❌   | HARD     |
456: | Context Verify   | ✅/❌   | HARD     |
457: 
458: **Gate Check:** ALL phases must show ✅. ANY ❌ = STOP and resolve.
459: ```
460: 
461: ### Violation Self-Detection
462: 
463: Every workflow command with blocking phases MUST include:
464: 
465: ```markdown
466: ## VIOLATION SELF-DETECTION (BLOCKING)
467: 
468: **Before proceeding, verify you have NOT:**
469: - [ ] Skipped any required phase
470: - [ ] Used project tools before completing phases
471: - [ ] Proceeded without required user confirmation
472: 
473: **If ANY violation:** STOP → State violation → Return to phase → Complete properly
474: ```
475: 
476: ### Gate Exemption Declaration
477: 
478: For commands exempt from Gate 3:
479: 
480: ```markdown
481: ## GATE 3 STATUS: EXEMPT
482: 
483: | Aspect      | Value                            |
484: | ----------- | -------------------------------- |
485: | Location    | [Where output goes]              |
486: | Reason      | [Why exempt]                     |
487: | Alternative | [What replaces spec folder]      |
488: ```

712: \`\`\`
713: 
714: **Example 2: [Another use case]**
715: \`\`\`
716: /workflow-name [different arguments]
717: \`\`\`
718: ```
719: 
720: ---
721: 
722: ## 11. MODE-BASED COMMAND TEMPLATE
723: 
724: Use for: Commands supporting `:auto` and `:confirm` execution modes.
725: 
726: ```markdown
727: ---
728: description: [Workflow name] ([N] steps) - [purpose]. Supports :auto and :confirm modes
729: argument-hint: "<request> [:auto|:confirm]"
730: allowed-tools: Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Task
731: ---
732: 
733: # [Command Title]
734: 
735: **Purpose**: [Description of what this command accomplishes.]
736: 
737: ### 🚨 MANDATORY FIRST ACTION - DO NOT SKIP
738: 
739: [Include the Mandatory Gate Pattern]
740: 
741: ---
742: 
743: ## 1. USER INPUT
744: 
745: \`\`\`text
746: $ARGUMENTS
747: \`\`\`
748: 
749: ---
750: 
751: ## 2. MODE DETECTION & ROUTING
752: 
753: ### Step 1: Parse Mode Suffix
754: 
755: Detect execution mode from command invocation:
756: 
757: | Pattern                | Mode        | Behavior                                      |
758: | ---------------------- | ----------- | --------------------------------------------- |
759: | `/command:auto`        | AUTONOMOUS  | Execute all steps without user approval gates |
760: | `/command:confirm`     | INTERACTIVE | Pause at each step for user approval          |
761: | `/command` (no suffix) | PROMPT      | Ask user to choose mode                       |
762: 
763: ### Step 2: Mode Selection (when no suffix detected)
764: 
765: If no `:auto` or `:confirm` suffix is present, present options to user:
766: 
767: **Question**: "How would you like to execute this workflow?"
768: 
769: | Option | Mode        | Description                                                    |
770: | ------ | ----------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
771: | **A**  | Autonomous  | Execute all steps without approval gates. Best for [use case]. |
772: | **B**  | Interactive | Pause at each step for approval. Best for [use case].          |
773: 
774: **Wait for user response before proceeding.**
775: 
776: ### Step 3: Transform Raw Input
777: 
778: Parse the raw text from `$ARGUMENTS` and transform into structured fields.
779: 
780: ---
781: 
782: ## 3. KEY BEHAVIORS
783: 
784: ### Autonomous Mode (`:auto`)
785: - Executes all steps without user approval gates
786: - Self-validates at each checkpoint
787: - Makes informed decisions based on best judgment
788: - Documents all significant decisions
789: 
790: ### Interactive Mode (`:confirm`)
791: - Pauses after each step for user approval
792: - Presents options: Approve, Review Details, Modify, Skip, Abort
793: - Documents user decisions at each checkpoint
794: - Allows course correction throughout workflow
795: 
796: ---
797: 
798: ## 4. CONTEXT LOADING
799: 
800: When resuming work in an existing spec folder, prompt to load prior session memory:
801: - **A)** Load most recent memory file (quick context refresh)
802: - **B)** Load all recent files (up to 3) (comprehensive context)
803: - **C)** List all files and select specific (historical search)
804: - **D)** Skip (start fresh, no context)
805: 
806: ---
807: 
808: ## 5. EXAMPLES
809: 
810: **Example 1: Autonomous execution**
811: \`\`\`
812: /command:auto [arguments]
813: \`\`\`
814: 
815: **Example 2: Interactive execution**
816: \`\`\`
817: /command:confirm [arguments]
818: \`\`\`
819: 
820: **Example 3: Prompt for mode selection**
821: \`\`\`
822: /command [arguments]
823: \`\`\`
824: ```
825: 
826: ### Presentation / Router Split (Command Families)
827: 
828: The memory, speckit, create, doctor, and deep command families split each command into a **thin router** plus **owned assets**, so routing logic and presentation contracts evolve independently and long command files stay readable.
829: 
830: **Common core across all split families:**
831: 
832: | Asset | Owns |
833: |-------|------|
834: | `<command>.md` (thin router) | Mode resolution, owned-assets table, routing logic, and any Phase 0 / mandatory-input gate. Contains NO presentation content. |
835: | `assets/<ns>-<command>-presentation.txt` | Startup prompts, dashboards and checkpoints, result templates, and next-step wording. The display source of truth. |
836: 
837: - The router contains a **Presentation Boundary** section naming what lives only in the presentation asset. It must contain no inline startup-question wording, dashboard templates, or result templates. The split is behavior-preserving, so relocate display content and never change routing semantics.
838: - In `allowed-tools`, MCP tools use the fully-qualified `mcp__<server>__<tool>` form (e.g. `mcp__code_mode__call_tool_chain`), matching the `opencode.json` MCP namespace. Bare tool IDs (e.g. `advisor_recommend`) belong in instruction prose, never in `allowed-tools`.
839: 
840: **Workflow-backed families (speckit, create, deep)** additionally own `:auto` / `:confirm` workflow YAML that the router routes modes to:
841: 
842: | Asset | Owns |
843: |-------|------|
844: | `assets/<ns>-<command>-auto.yaml` | Autonomous-mode workflow: steps, agent dispatch, artifact writes. |
845: | `assets/<ns>-<command>-confirm.yaml` | Interactive-mode workflow. |
846: 
847: The **memory** and **doctor** families have NO workflow YAML. Their routers dispatch directly to tools and scripts.
848: 
849: **Canonical router shape (first-class standard).** Every router uses one canonical, numbered section vocabulary of full integers, in this order: **`## 1. ROUTER CONTRACT`**, **`## 2. OWNED ASSETS`**, **`## 3. MODE ROUTING`**, **`## 4. EXECUTION TARGETS`**, **`## 5. PRESENTATION BOUNDARY`**, **`## 6. WORKFLOW SUMMARY`**. The blocking core is only `Owned Assets` plus `Presentation Boundary`, and the other four are recommended and surface as non-blocking warnings when absent. Variants differ by hand-off only, not by required sections:
850: 
851: - **Workflow-YAML-backed** routers route modes into `-auto.yaml` / `-confirm.yaml`.
852: - **Direct-dispatch-script** routers dispatch straight to tools and scripts and may leave the recommended sections as warnings.
853: - **Compiled-stub** commands carry a `render-command-contract` marker and are exempt from section requirements (retained variant, no command currently uses it).
854: 
855: Which family uses which topology is defined by the machine-readable command contract ([`command-contract.json`](command-contract.json), validated by [`command-contract.schema.json`](command-contract.schema.json)). Read it rather than hand-maintaining a family list here.
856: 
857: Do not invent divergent synonyms (`Routing Assets`, `Workflow Routing`, `Execution Order`). The validator alias-normalizes those as a safety net, but the authored end state is the canonical names above. Reference shape: `.skilled/commands/speckit/plan.md` (router) + `speckit-plan-presentation.txt` (contract). Skeletons: [`command-router-template.md`](command-router-template.md), [`command-presentation-template.md`](command-presentation-template.md).
858: 
859: ---
860: 
861: ## 12. ARGUMENT DISPATCH PATTERN
862: 
863: Use for: Commands that accept multiple argument types and need to route to different actions.
864: 
865: ### Pattern Overview
866: 
867: When a single command handles multiple argument patterns (like `/semantic_search` accepting queries, actions, and flags), use an ASCII decision tree to document the routing logic clearly.
868: 
869: ### When to Use Argument Dispatch
870: 
871: | Scenario                                   | Use Pattern?                 |
872: | ------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------- |
873: | Command has multiple action keywords       | **Yes**                      |
874: | Command accepts both keywords AND queries  | **Yes**                      |
875: | Command has only one action                | No (use simple template)     |
876: | Command uses `:auto`/`:confirm` modes only | No (use mode-based template) |
877: 
878: ### The Pattern
879: 
880: ```markdown
881: ---
882: description: [Command] with multiple entry points
883: argument-hint: "[action|query] [options]"
884: allowed-tools: [Tools]
885: ---
886: 
887: # [Command Title]
888: 
889: ---
890: 
891: ## 1. ARGUMENT DISPATCH
892: 
893: \`\`\`
894: $ARGUMENTS
895:     │
896:     ├─► Empty (no args)
897:     │   └─► DEFAULT ACTION: [What happens with no args]
898:     │
899:     ├─► First word matches ACTION KEYWORD (case-insensitive)
900:     │   ├─► "start" | "on" | "init"       → START ACTION
901:     │   ├─► "stop" | "off" | "kill"       → STOP ACTION
902:     │   ├─► "status" | "info"             → STATUS ACTION
903:     │   ├─► "search" | "find" | "query"   → SEARCH ACTION (remaining args = query)
904:     │   └─► "reset" | "clear"             → RESET ACTION
905:     │
906:     ├─► Looks like NATURAL LANGUAGE QUERY
907:     │   Detection: 2+ words, question words, code terms, quotes
908:     │   └─► SEARCH ACTION (full args = query)
909:     │
910:     └─► Single ambiguous word
911:         └─► [DEFAULT ACTION] (assume most common intent)
912: \`\`\`
913: 
914: ---
915: 
916: ## 2. ACTION HANDLERS
917: 
918: ### START ACTION
919: [Instructions for start]
920: 
921: ### STOP ACTION
922: [Instructions for stop]
923: 
924: ### SEARCH ACTION
925: [Instructions for search]
926: 
927: ---
928: 
929: ## 3. EXAMPLE ROUTING
930: 
931: | Input                | Detected As      | Action                  |
932: | -------------------- | ---------------- | ----------------------- |
933: | (empty)              | No args          | Show menu/help          |
934: | `start`              | Keyword          | START ACTION            |
935: | `how does auth work` | Natural language | SEARCH ACTION           |
936: | `oauth`              | Single word      | SEARCH ACTION (default) |
937: ```
938: 
939: ### Real Example: `/semantic_search`
940: 
941: ```
942: /semantic_search [args]
943:     │
944:     ├─► No args
945:     │   └─► Show usage help
946:     │
947:     ├─► "index" | "reindex" | "rebuild"
948:     │   └─► INDEX ACTION: Rebuild vector index
949:     │
950:     ├─► "status" | "health"
951:     │   └─► STATUS ACTION: Show index health
952:     │
953:     ├─► Natural language query (2+ words)
954:     │   └─► SEARCH ACTION: Execute semantic search
955:     │
956:     └─► Single ambiguous word
957:         └─► SEARCH ACTION (assume search intent)
958: ```
959: 
960: ### Combining with Mode-Based Pattern
961: 
962: For commands that need BOTH argument dispatch AND mode support:
963: 
964: ```
965: $ARGUMENTS
966:     │
967:     ├─► Parse mode suffix (:auto | :confirm)
968:     │
969:     └─► After mode extraction, dispatch remaining args:
970:         ├─► "action1" → ACTION 1
971:         ├─► "action2" → ACTION 2
972:         └─► Natural language → DEFAULT ACTION
973: ```
974: 
975: ---
976: 
977: ## 13. DESTRUCTIVE COMMAND TEMPLATE
978: 
979: Use for: Commands that delete data or make irreversible changes.
980: 
981: ```markdown
982: ---
983: description: [Action] (DESTRUCTIVE)
984: argument-hint: "[--confirm]"
985: allowed-tools: Bash
986: ---
987: 
988: # [Command Title]
989: 
990: **DESTRUCTIVE OPERATION** - [Brief warning about what will be affected.]
991: 
992: ---
993: 
994: ## 1. PURPOSE
995: 
996: [Explain the destructive action and why it might be needed.]
997: 
998: ---
999: 
1000: ## 2. CONTRACT
1001: 
1002: **Inputs:** `$ARGUMENTS`, which must include the `--confirm` flag to skip the prompt
1003: **Outputs:** `STATUS=<OK|FAIL|CANCELLED> ACTION=<action|cancelled>`
1004: 
1005: ---
1006: 
1007: ## 3. INSTRUCTIONS
1008: 
1009: ### Step 1: Safety Check - Require Confirmation
1010: 
1011: - Check if `--confirm` flag is present in `$ARGUMENTS`
1012: - If NOT present:
1013:   - Ask user: "[Warning message]. Are you sure?"
1014:   - Options: "Yes, proceed" / "No, cancel"
1015:   - If user cancels: `STATUS=CANCELLED ACTION=cancelled`
1016: 
1017: ### Step 2: Show What Will Be Affected
1018: 
1019: - Display current state
1020: - List items that will be deleted/changed
1021: - Show size/count of affected data
1022: 
1023: ### Step 3: Execute Destructive Action
1024: 
1025: - [Step-by-step execution]
1026: - Log each action taken
1027: 
1028: ### Step 4: Verify Completion
1029: 
1030: - Confirm action completed
1031: - Show new state
1032: 
1033: ### Step 5: Provide Recovery Guidance
1034: 
1035: - Explain how to rebuild/restore if needed
1036: - Link to relevant commands
1037: 
1038: ### Step 6: Return Status
1039: 
1040: - If completed: `STATUS=OK ACTION=[action]`
1041: - If cancelled: `STATUS=CANCELLED ACTION=cancelled`
1042: - If failed: `STATUS=FAIL ERROR="<message>"`
1043: 
1044: ---
1045: 
1046: ## 4. EXAMPLE USAGE
1047: 
1048: ### Without Confirmation (Safe Default)
1049: 
1050: \`\`\`bash
1051: /command-name
1052: \`\`\`
1053: → Will prompt for confirmation before proceeding
1054: 
1055: ### With Confirmation Flag (Skip Prompt)
1056: 
1057: \`\`\`bash
1058: /command-name --confirm
1059: \`\`\`
1060: → Proceeds immediately (use with caution)
1061: 
1062: ---
1063: 
1064: ## 5. NOTES
1065: 
1066: - **When to Use:**
1067:   - [Valid use case 1]
1068:   - [Valid use case 2]
1069: 
1070: - **Impact:**
1071:   - [What will be lost]
1072:   - [Other consequences]
1073:   - [What is preserved]
1074:   - [Recovery options]
1075: 
1076: - **Alternatives to Consider:**
1077:   - [Less destructive alternative]
1078:   - [Another option]
1079: 
1080: ---
1081: 
1082: ## 6. SAFETY FEATURES
1083: 
1084: - Requires explicit confirmation by default
1085: - Shows what will be affected before proceeding
1086: - Provides clear recovery steps
1087: - Cannot accidentally affect [protected items]
1088: ```
1089: 
1090: ---
1091: 
1092: ## 14. NAMESPACE COMMAND PATTERN
1093: 
1094: Use for: Grouping related commands under a common prefix.
1095: 
1096: ### Directory Structure
1097: 
1098: ```
1099: .skilled/commands/
1100: └── [namespace]/           # Directory name = namespace
1101:     ├── [action1].md       # → /namespace:action1
1102:     ├── [action2].md       # → /namespace:action2
1103:     └── [action3].md       # → /namespace:action3
1104: ```
1105: 
1106: ### Example: Index Namespace
1107: 
1108: ```
1109: .skilled/commands/
1110: └── index/
1111:     ├── start.md     → /index:start
1112:     ├── stop.md      → /index:stop
1113:     ├── search.md    → /index:search
1114:     ├── stats.md     → /index:stats
1115:     ├── history.md   → /index:history
1116:     └── reset.md     → /index:reset
1117: ```
1118: 
1119: ### Naming Conventions
1120: 
1121: | Element             | Convention             | Example                      |
1122: | ------------------- | ---------------------- | ---------------------------- |
1123: | Namespace directory | lowercase, hyphen-case | `index/`, `git-workflow/`    |
1124: | Action files        | lowercase, hyphen-case | `search.md`, `full-reset.md` |
1125: | Resulting command   | namespace:action       | `/index:search`              |
1126: 
1127: Namespace and action segments must match `^[a-z0-9]+(?:-[a-z0-9]+)*$`. Reject underscore-bearing or ambiguous names, and keep each emitted `.md` stem identical to its validated action.
1128: 
1129: ---
1130: 
1131: ## 15. VALIDATION CHECKLIST
1132: 
1133: Before publishing a command, verify:
1134: 
1135: ### Frontmatter
1136: 
1137: - [ ] `description` is present and action-oriented
1138: - [ ] `argument-hint` shows expected format (if args expected)
1139: - [ ] `allowed-tools` lists all tools used (if any)
1140: - [ ] No angle brackets `< >` in description (reserved for hints)
1141: 
1142: ### Mandatory Gate (CRITICAL for required arguments)
1143: 
1144: - [ ] If `argument-hint` contains `<required>` args → **MANDATORY GATE present**
1145: - [ ] Gate sits **after the H1 and its purpose line**, before any workflow step
1146: - [ ] Gate presents options to user with appropriate question
1147: - [ ] Gate includes all 4 CRITICAL RULES (DO NOT infer, assume, proceed)
1148: - [ ] Skip gate only if ALL arguments are `[optional]` with defaults
1149: 
1150: ### Structure
1151: 
1152: - [ ] H1 title matches command purpose
1153: - [ ] H2 sections use format: `## N. SECTION-NAME` (see the Section Vocabulary)
1154: - [ ] H3 subsections: `### Step N: Description`
1155: - [ ] Dividers (`---`) between major sections
1156: - [ ] Instructions are numbered and actionable
1157: - [ ] Example usage shows 2-3 scenarios
1158: - [ ] Full integer step numbering only (no 1.5, 2.5 - see Section 5)
1159: 
1160: ### Header Format
1161: 
1162: - [ ] H1: Plain title only (`# Command Title`) or with semantic emoji for blocking sections (`# 🚨 MANDATORY PHASES`)
1163: - [ ] H2: Numbered + SECTION-NAME (`## 1. PURPOSE`)
1164: - [ ] H3/H4: Title case (`### Step 1: Description`)
1165: - [ ] Consistent numbering (1, 2, 3...)
1166: - [ ] Section names from approved vocabulary (see the Section Vocabulary)
1167: 
1168: **Blocking Phase Pattern:**
1169: Commands with mandatory input phases use these semantic markers:
1170: - `# MANDATORY PHASES` - Critical blocking section (H1)
1171: - `## PHASE N:` - Required blocking phases (H2)
1172: - `## PHASE STATUS VERIFICATION` - Gate checks (H2)
1173: - `## VIOLATION SELF-DETECTION` - Violation recovery (H2)
1174: 
1175: ---
1176: 
1177: ## 16. ORCHESTRATOR + WORKERS PATTERN
1178: 
1179: Use for: Commands that spawn parallel sub-agents for exploration/analysis.
1180: 
1181: ```
1182: OPUS ORCHESTRATOR → Dispatches → SONNET WORKERS (parallel)
1183:      │                              │
1184:      └── Synthesizes ←──────────────┘
1185: ```
1186: 
1187: | Role             | Model    | Responsibility                                        |
1188: | ---------------- | -------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
1189: | **Orchestrator** | `opus`   | Task understanding, dispatch, verification, synthesis |
1190: | **Workers**      | `sonnet` | Fast parallel exploration, hypothesis generation      |
1191: 
1192: **Use when**: Parallel codebase exploration, multi-aspect analysis, complex planning.
1193: **Skip when**: Simple single-action commands, sequential workflows.
1194: 
1195: ---
1196: 
1197: ## 17. STATUS OUTPUT PATTERNS
1198: 
1199: ### Standard Patterns
1200: 
1201: | Pattern                                 | Use Case       | Example              |
1202: | --------------------------------------- | -------------- | -------------------- |
1203: | `STATUS=OK`                             | Simple success | Basic commands       |
1204: | `STATUS=OK RESULTS_COUNT=N`             | Search/query   | `/index:search`      |
1205: | `STATUS=OK ACTION=<action>`             | State change   | `/index:start`       |
1206: | `STATUS=OK ACTION=<action> PATH=<path>` | File creation  | `/speckit:complete` |
1207: | `STATUS=FAIL ERROR="<message>"`         | All failures   | Error handling       |
1208: | `STATUS=CANCELLED ACTION=cancelled`     | User abort     | Interactive commands |
1209: 
1210: ---
1211: 
1212: ## 18. BEST PRACTICES SUMMARY
1213: 
1214: ### DO
1215: 
1216: | Practice                                 | Reason                            |
1217: | ---------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
1218: | Include mandatory gate for required args | Prevents context inference errors |
1219: | Use action verbs in descriptions         | Clear, scannable in /help         |
1220: | Document all steps with checkpoints      | Enables debugging and recovery    |
1221: | Provide example usage                    | Users learn faster                |
1222: | Return structured status                 | Enables automation                |
1223: | Use appropriate command type             | Right tool for the job            |
1224: 
1225: ### DON'T
1226: 
1227: | Anti-Pattern               | Problem                      |
1228: | -------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
1229: | Skip mandatory gate        | AI will infer incorrectly    |
1230: | Vague descriptions         | Users won't know when to use |
1231: | Missing error handling     | Failures become mysterious   |
1232: | No examples                | Users struggle to start      |
1233: | Inconsistent status format | Breaks automation            |
1234: | Over-complex commands      | Split into namespace instead |
1235: 
1236: ---
1237: 
1238: ## 19. RELATED RESOURCES
1239:

1241: - [frontmatter-templates.md](../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) - Frontmatter by document type
1242: - [skill-md-template.md](../../sk-create-skill/assets/skill/skill-md-template.md) - If converting to skill
1243: 
1244: ### Standards
1245: - [core-standards.md](../../shared/references/core-standards.md) - Document type rules
1246: - [validation.md](../../shared/references/validation.md) - Quality scoring
1247: - [command-contract.json](command-contract.json) / [command-contract.schema.json](command-contract.schema.json) - Machine-readable behavioral contract and its schema
1248: 
1249: ---
1250: 
1251: ## 20. COMMAND CONTRACT
1252: 
1253: Behavioral truth per family, meaning topology, input and gate owner, execution targets, mode matrix,
1254: owned assets, presentation ownership with typed exceptions, destructive policy, timeout bounds,
1255: and invocation aliases, is defined once in the machine-readable contract
1256: [`command-contract.json`](command-contract.json), validated against
1257: [`command-contract.schema.json`](command-contract.schema.json). This template's prose describes
1258: how to author a command. The contract is the source of truth for what each family does. Read the
1259: contract for a family's authoritative topology and mode default rather than re-deriving it from a
1260: hand-maintained list. A single family entry validates as one `familyContract`:
1261: 
1262: <!-- contract-example -->
1263: ```json
1264: {
1265:   "topology": "direct-dispatch",
1266:   "router_path": ".skilled/commands/<ns>/<action>.md",
1267:   "input": { "required": false, "gate_owner": "router", "argument_hint": "<query> | <sub-action>" },
1268:   "execution_targets": [
1269:     { "selector": "<sub-action>", "target": "the tool, script, or MCP call the router dispatches" }
1270:   ],
1271:   "mode_matrix": { "default_policy": "non-mutating-default", "supported_modes": [] },
1272:   "owned_assets": [
1273:     { "purpose": "presentation", "path": ".skilled/commands/<ns>/assets/<action>-presentation.txt" }
1274:   ],
1275:   "presentation": { "owner": "presentation-asset", "exceptions": [] },
1276:   "destructive_policy": { "has_destructive_ops": true, "gated": true, "operations": ["names the destructive operations and confirms they are gated"] },
1277:   "invocation_aliases": ["/<ns>:<action>"]
1278: }
1279: ```

20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### What Are OpenCode Commands?
23: 
24: **OpenCode commands** are slash-triggered instructions (e.g., `/speckit:complete`, `/speckit:save`) that automate workflows, enforce patterns, and extend AI agent capabilities. They're markdown files that define structured behavior for specific tasks.
25: 
26: **Core Purpose**:
27: - **Workflow automation** - Multi-step processes become single invocations
28: - **Pattern enforcement** - Consistent behavior across sessions
29: - **Task routing** - Arguments dispatch to appropriate handlers
30: - **User guidance** - Structured prompts prevent errors
31: - **Tool restriction** - Limit which tools the command can use
32: 
33: **Key Difference from Skills**:
34: - Commands = Actionable workflows triggered by `/command-name`
35: - Skills = Reference documentation loaded via `Read(".skilled/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md")`
36: 
37: ### Core Characteristics
38: 
39: | Characteristic         | Description                                           |
40: | ---------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
41: | **Markdown-based**     | Human-readable instruction files                      |
42: | **Frontmatter-driven** | Metadata controls behavior (description, args, tools) |
43: | **Argument-aware**     | Parse and validate user input via `$ARGUMENTS`        |
44: | **Status-reporting**   | Return structured outcomes (`STATUS=OK\|FAIL`)        |
45: | **Tool-restricted**    | `allowed-tools` limits available tools                |
46: 
47: ### How Commands Are Invoked
48: 
49: ```
50: User types: /command-name arguments
51:                 │           │
52:                 │           └─► Passed as $ARGUMENTS variable
53:                 │
54:                 └─► OpenCode finds .opencode/commands/command-name.md
55:                     │
56:                     ├─► Loads frontmatter (description, tools, hints)
57:                     │
58:                     ├─► Injects $ARGUMENTS into instruction body
59:                     │
60:                     └─► AI agent executes instructions step-by-step
61: ```
62: 
63: > **Description budget**: command `description:` fields share the Claude Code skill-metadata budget (default 8,000 chars total). Keep each command description **≤ 110 chars**, retain `:auto`/`:confirm` mode suffixes (advisor trigger tokens), no product enumerations. See [`assets/frontmatter-templates.md` § Description Budget & Trim Style](../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for the canonical trim rules.
64: 
65: ### Command File Location
66: 
67: ```
68: .skilled/
69: └── command/
70:     ├── simple-command.md          → /simple-command
71:     ├── workflow-command.md        → /workflow-command
72:     └── namespace/                  → Grouped commands
73:         ├── action1.md             → /namespace:action1
74:         └── action2.md             → /namespace:action2
75: ```
76: 
77: ### Progressive Complexity
78: 
79: ```
80: Level 1: Simple Command
81:          └─ Single action, few arguments (~50-100 lines)
82:             ↓
83: Level 2: Workflow Command
84:          └─ Multi-step process with validation (~100-200 lines)
85:             ↓
86: Level 3: Mode-Based / Dispatch Command
87:          └─ Complex routing, user control (~150-300 lines)
88: ```
89:

92: ## 2. WHEN TO CREATE COMMANDS
93: 
94: ### Create Command When
95: 
96: - Multi-step process with defined phases
97: - Repeated task needing consistency across sessions
98: - Requires confirmation gates (destructive actions)
99: - Multiple argument patterns need routing
100: - User should control execution pace (`:auto`/`:confirm` modes)
101: - Tool restrictions needed for security/focus
102: 
103: ### Use Skill Instead When
104: 
105: - Content is reference material, not executable workflow
106: - Complex domain knowledge that multiple commands might need
107: - Reusable patterns/standards across multiple commands
108: 
109: ### Decision Framework
110: 
111: ```
112: Is this a repeatable workflow with defined steps?
113: ├─► YES
114: │   │
115: │   ├─► Does it need user arguments?
116: │   │   └─► Command with argument-hint + mandatory gate
117: │   │
118: │   ├─► Does it have modes (auto/confirm)?
119: │   │   └─► Mode-based command template
120: │   │
121: │   ├─► Is it destructive/irreversible?
122: │   │   └─► Destructive command template
123: │   │
124: │   ├─► Multiple action keywords (start/stop/status)?
125: │   │   └─► Argument dispatch pattern
126: │   │
127: │   └─► Simple single action?
128: │       └─► Simple command template
129: │
130: └─► NO
131:     │
132:     ├─► Is it reference documentation?
133:     │   └─► Create Skill instead
134:     │
135:     ├─► Is it reusable knowledge?
136:     │   └─► Create Skill instead
137:     │
138:     └─► Is it one-time task?
139:         └─► Just do it (no command needed)
140: ```
141: 
142: ### Command Types by Complexity
143: 
144: | Type                  | Complexity | Lines       | Use When                                 |
145: | --------------------- | ---------- | ----------- | ---------------------------------------- |
146: | **Simple**            | Low        | 50-100      | Single action, few args                  |
147: | **Workflow**          | Medium     | 100-200     | Multi-step process with outputs          |
148: | **Mode-Based**        | Medium     | 150-250     | User controls execution pace             |
149: | **Argument Dispatch** | Medium     | 150-300     | Multiple entry points/actions            |
150: | **Destructive**       | Medium     | 100-180     | Irreversible actions, needs confirmation |
151: | **Namespace**         | Varies     | 50-150 each | Related commands grouped together        |

194: ## 4. STANDARD COMMAND STRUCTURE
195: 
196: ### Common Sections (All Command Types)
197: 
198: | Order | Section             | Required         | Purpose                             |
199: | ----- | ------------------- | ---------------- | ----------------------------------- |
200: | 0     | **Frontmatter**     | Yes              | Metadata (description, args, tools) |
201: | 1     | **Mandatory Gate**  | If required args | Prevent context inference           |
202: | 2     | **Title + Purpose** | Yes              | What the command does               |
203: | 3     | **Contract**        | Recommended      | Inputs/outputs specification        |
204: | 4     | **Instructions**    | Yes              | Step-by-step execution              |
205: | 5     | **Examples**        | Recommended      | Usage demonstrations                |
206: | 6     | **Notes**           | Optional         | Caveats, requirements               |
207: 
208: > **Frontmatter budget:** keep `argument-hint` at or under 140 characters. It **summarizes** the invocation shape while the router's **EXECUTION TARGETS** section **enumerates** the full flag surface. Over-budget hints warn, they never block registration.
209: 
210: ### Minimal Command Structure
211: 
212: ```markdown
213: ---
214: description: [Action verb] [what it does]
215: argument-hint: "<required> [optional]"
216: allowed-tools: Tool1, Tool2
217: ---
218: 
219: # Command Title
220: 
221: [One sentence describing purpose.]
222: 
223: <!-- REQUIRED-ARGUMENT GATE: keep this block whenever argument-hint declares a required
224: <argument>. Delete it only for a command that takes none. It is the reason a command stops
225: instead of inventing an input from context. -->
226: 
227: ### MANDATORY INPUT GATE
228: 
229: **STATUS: BLOCKED** until `<required>` is bound.
230: 
231: 1. Parse `$ARGUMENTS`, stripping any mode suffix and flags before resolving the required input.
232: 2. Treat an absent or whitespace-only value as missing. Do not infer it from conversation
233:    history, open files, screenshots, or repository state.
234: 3. When it is missing, ask for it with clear options or an expected reply format, stop, and
235:    wait. Use only `$ARGUMENTS` or that explicit reply.
236: 
237: ## 1. PURPOSE
238: 
239: [2-3 sentences explaining the command.]
240: 
241: ## 2. INSTRUCTIONS
242: 
243: ### Step 1: [Name]
244: [Instructions]
245: 
246: ### Step 2: Return Status
247: - Success: `STATUS=OK`
248: - Failure: `STATUS=FAIL ERROR="<message>"`
249: ```
250: 
251: ---
252: 
253: ## 5. STEP NUMBERING RULES
254: 
255: **Rule**: Use full integers only (1, 2, 3). No decimals (1.5, 2.5) or sub-steps (1.1, 1.2).
256: 
257: | Element  | Correct                   | Wrong              |
258: | -------- | ------------------------- | ------------------ |
259: | Steps    | Step 1, Step 2, Step 3    | Step 1.5, Step 2.5 |
260: | Phases   | PHASE 1, PHASE 2, PHASE 3 | PHASE 1.5, PHASE 2 |
261: | Sections | ## 1. PURPOSE               | ## 1.1 PURPOSE     |
262: 
263: **Sub-activities**: Use bullets within a step, not decimal sub-steps:
264: ```markdown
265: Step 3: Execute workflow
266:   - Load configuration
267:   - Validate inputs  
268:   - Run process
269: ```
270: 
271: ---
272: 
273: ## 6. SECTION VOCABULARY
274: 
275: Commands use two categories of notation: **semantic markers** (for blocking/validation states) and **section names** (for content organization).
276: 
277: ### Semantic Markers (Blocking/Validation)
278: 
279: These markers indicate workflow state and enforcement:
280: 
281: | Marker | Name    | Purpose                     | Example Usage               |
282: | ------ | ------- | --------------------------- | --------------------------- |
283: | MANDATORY | Alert   | Critical/mandatory sections | `# MANDATORY PHASES`      |
284: | PHASE  | Lock    | Phase/gate headers          | `## PHASE 1: INPUT`       |
285: | PASSED | Check   | Passed/success status       | `PASSED`                   |
286: | N/A    | Skip    | N/A or skipped              | `N/A (no memory files)`    |
287: | STOP   | Stop    | Hard stop/blocking error    | `STOP - Phase incomplete`  |
288: | WARNING| Warning | Non-blocking alert          | `VIOLATION DETECTED`       |
289: | FAILED | Fail    | Validation failure          | `FAILED`                   |
290: 
291: ### Standard Section Names
292: 
293: These names identify section types. Use EXACTLY as shown:
294: 
295: | Section      | H2 Format                    | Purpose                      |
296: | ------------ | ---------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
297: | PURPOSE      | `## N. PURPOSE`              | What the command does        |
298: | CONTRACT     | `## N. CONTRACT`             | Inputs/outputs specification |
299: | WORKFLOW     | `## N. WORKFLOW OVERVIEW`    | Process flow/steps table     |
300: | INSTRUCTIONS | `## N. INSTRUCTIONS`         | How to execute               |
301: | REFERENCE    | `## N. REFERENCE`            | Related resources            |
302: | EXAMPLES     | `## N. EXAMPLES`             | Usage demonstrations         |
303: | RELATED      | `## N. RELATED COMMANDS`     | Links to related commands    |
304: | TOOLS        | `## N. TOOL SIGNATURES`      | MCP/tool configuration       |
305: | ROUTING      | `## N. ARGUMENT ROUTING`     | Mode detection/dispatch      |
306: | DOCS         | `## N. FULL DOCUMENTATION`   | Link to full docs            |
307: | INPUT        | `## N. USER INPUT`           | User input display           |
308: 
309: ### Section Naming Rules
310: 
311: 1. **One name per purpose**: Don't reuse section names across different purposes
312: 2. **Consistent naming**: Use the same section name for the same purpose across commands
313: 3. **Exact format**: `## N. SECTION-NAME` (number, period, space, name in ALL CAPS)
314:

317: ## 7. FRONTMATTER REFERENCE
318: 
319: ### Required Fields
320: 
321: ```yaml
322: ---
323: description: Clear, action-oriented single-line description shown in /help output. Start with action verb (Create, Search, Delete, Start, Stop).
324: ---
325: ```
326: 
327: > **Important:** The `description` field MUST be a single-line string, not a YAML block scalar (`|` or `>`). Multi-line descriptions break `/help` output rendering.
328: 
329: ### Recommended Fields
330: 
331: ```yaml
332: ---
333: argument-hint: "<required> [optional] [--flag]"
334: # Format conventions:
335: #   <angle-brackets> = required argument
336: #   [square-brackets] = optional argument
337: #   --flag = boolean flag
338: #   [default: value] = argument with default
339: 
340: allowed-tools: Tool1, Tool2, Tool3
341: # Common tools: Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob, Task
342: # MCP tools: mcp__[server-name]__[tool_function]
343: ---
344: ```
345: 
346: ### Optional Fields
347: 
348: ```yaml
349: ---
350: name: command-name
351: # Override inferred name from filename
352: 
353: model: opus
354: # Override default model (USE SPARINGLY - only for complex reasoning)
355: 
356: version: 1.0.0
357: # Track command version
358: 
359: disable-model-invocation: true
360: # Prevent the AI agent from invoking this command
361: ---
362: ```
363: 
364: ### Example
365: 
366: ```yaml
367: ---
368: description: Complete spec folder workflow (5 steps) - research through implementation
369: argument-hint: "<task> [:auto|:confirm]"
370: allowed-tools: Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Task
371: ---
372: ```

376: ## 8. MANDATORY GATE PATTERN (CRITICAL)
377: 
378: ### Why This Pattern Exists
379: 
380: Without this gate, AI agents may:
381: - Infer tasks from conversation history or open files
382: - Assume what the user wants based on screenshots or context
383: - Proceed with incorrect assumptions instead of asking
384: 
385: ### When to Use
386: 
387: | Argument Type                  | Use Mandatory Gate? | Example                              |
388: | ------------------------------ | ------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
389: | `<required>` (angle brackets)  | **YES**             | `<task>`, `<query>`, `<spec-folder>` |
390: | `[optional]` (square brackets) | No (has default)    | `[count]`, `[--flag]`                |
391: | `[:auto\|:confirm]` mode flags | No (mode selection) | Mode suffixes only                   |
392: 
393: ### The Pattern
394: 
395: Add this block **after the H1 and its purpose line, before any workflow step**:
396: 
397: ```markdown
398: ### 🚨 MANDATORY FIRST ACTION - DO NOT SKIP
399: 
400: **BEFORE ANY WORKFLOW STEP, CHECK `$ARGUMENTS`:**
401: 
402: \`\`\`
403: IF $ARGUMENTS is empty, undefined, or contains only whitespace (ignoring mode flags):
404:     → STOP IMMEDIATELY
405:     → Present the user with this question:
406:         question: "[Context-appropriate question]"
407:         options:
408:           - label: "[Action label]"
409:             description: "[What user will provide]"
410:     → WAIT for user response
411:     → Use their response as the [input type]
412:     → Only THEN continue with this workflow
413: 
414: IF $ARGUMENTS contains [expected input]:
415:     → Continue reading this file
416: \`\`\`
417: 
418: **CRITICAL RULES:**
419: - **DO NOT** infer [input type] from context, screenshots, or existing files
420: - **DO NOT** assume what the user wants based on conversation history
421: - **DO NOT** proceed past this point without an explicit [input] from the user
422: - The [input] MUST come from `$ARGUMENTS` or user's answer to the question above
423: ```
424: 
425: ### Example Questions by Command Type
426: 
427: | Command Purpose    | Question                                          |
428: | ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------- |
429: | Planning           | "What would you like to plan?"                    |
430: | Research           | "What topic would you like to research?"          |
431: | Implementation     | "Which spec folder would you like to implement?"  |
432: | File improvement   | "What would you like to improve and which files?" |
433: | Prompt enhancement | "What prompt would you like to improve?"          |
434: | Generic routing    | "What request would you like to route?"           |
435: 
436: ### Multi-Phase Blocking Pattern
437: 
438: For commands requiring multiple inputs before workflow execution:
439: 
440: ```markdown
441: # 🚨 MANDATORY PHASES - BLOCKING ENFORCEMENT
442: 
443: > **HARD BLOCK**: Do not proceed past this section until ALL phases complete.
444: 
445: ## PHASE 1: INPUT COLLECTION
446: [Collect required inputs from $ARGUMENTS or prompt user]
447: 
448: ## PHASE 2: CONTEXT VERIFICATION
449: [Verify prerequisites exist]
450: 
451: ## PHASE STATUS VERIFICATION (BLOCKING)
452: 
453: | Phase            | Status | Blocker? |
454: | ---------------- | ------ | -------- |
455: | Input Collection | ✅/❌   | HARD     |
456: | Context Verify   | ✅/❌   | HARD     |
457: 
458: **Gate Check:** ALL phases must show ✅. ANY ❌ = STOP and resolve.
459: ```
460: 
461: ### Violation Self-Detection
462: 
463: Every workflow command with blocking phases MUST include:
464: 
465: ```markdown
466: ## VIOLATION SELF-DETECTION (BLOCKING)
467: 
468: **Before proceeding, verify you have NOT:**
469: - [ ] Skipped any required phase
470: - [ ] Used project tools before completing phases
471: - [ ] Proceeded without required user confirmation
472: 
473: **If ANY violation:** STOP → State violation → Return to phase → Complete properly
474: ```
475: 
476: ### Gate Exemption Declaration
477: 
478: For commands exempt from Gate 3:
479: 
480: ```markdown
481: ## GATE 3 STATUS: EXEMPT
482: 
483: | Aspect      | Value                            |
484: | ----------- | -------------------------------- |
485: | Location    | [Where output goes]              |
486: | Reason      | [Why exempt]                     |
487: | Alternative | [What replaces spec folder]      |
488: ```

743: ## 1. USER INPUT

745: \`\`\`text
746: $ARGUMENTS
747: \`\`\`

751: ## 2. MODE DETECTION & ROUTING
752: 
753: ### Step 1: Parse Mode Suffix
754: 
755: Detect execution mode from command invocation:
756: 
757: | Pattern                | Mode        | Behavior                                      |
758: | ---------------------- | ----------- | --------------------------------------------- |
759: | `/command:auto`        | AUTONOMOUS  | Execute all steps without user approval gates |
760: | `/command:confirm`     | INTERACTIVE | Pause at each step for user approval          |
761: | `/command` (no suffix) | PROMPT      | Ask user to choose mode                       |
762: 
763: ### Step 2: Mode Selection (when no suffix detected)
764: 
765: If no `:auto` or `:confirm` suffix is present, present options to user:
766: 
767: **Question**: "How would you like to execute this workflow?"
768: 
769: | Option | Mode        | Description                                                    |
770: | ------ | ----------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
771: | **A**  | Autonomous  | Execute all steps without approval gates. Best for [use case]. |
772: | **B**  | Interactive | Pause at each step for approval. Best for [use case].          |
773: 
774: **Wait for user response before proceeding.**
775: 
776: ### Step 3: Transform Raw Input
777: 
778: Parse the raw text from `$ARGUMENTS` and transform into structured fields.
779: 
780: ---
781: 
782: ## 3. KEY BEHAVIORS
783: 
784: ### Autonomous Mode (`:auto`)
785: - Executes all steps without user approval gates
786: - Self-validates at each checkpoint
787: - Makes informed decisions based on best judgment
788: - Documents all significant decisions
789: 
790: ### Interactive Mode (`:confirm`)
791: - Pauses after each step for user approval
792: - Presents options: Approve, Review Details, Modify, Skip, Abort
793: - Documents user decisions at each checkpoint
794: - Allows course correction throughout workflow
795: 
796: ---

798: ## 4. CONTEXT LOADING
799: 
800: When resuming work in an existing spec folder, prompt to load prior session memory:
801: - **A)** Load most recent memory file (quick context refresh)
802: - **B)** Load all recent files (up to 3) (comprehensive context)
803: - **C)** List all files and select specific (historical search)
804: - **D)** Skip (start fresh, no context)

817: /command:confirm [arguments]

826: ### Presentation / Router Split (Command Families)
827: 
828: The memory, speckit, create, doctor, and deep command families split each command into a **thin router** plus **owned assets**, so routing logic and presentation contracts evolve independently and long command files stay readable.
829: 
830: **Common core across all split families:**
831: 
832: | Asset | Owns |
833: |-------|------|
834: | `<command>.md` (thin router) | Mode resolution, owned-assets table, routing logic, and any Phase 0 / mandatory-input gate. Contains NO presentation content. |
835: | `assets/<ns>-<command>-presentation.txt` | Startup prompts, dashboards and checkpoints, result templates, and next-step wording. The display source of truth. |
836: 
837: - The router contains a **Presentation Boundary** section naming what lives only in the presentation asset. It must contain no inline startup-question wording, dashboard templates, or result templates. The split is behavior-preserving, so relocate display content and never change routing semantics.
838: - In `allowed-tools`, MCP tools use the fully-qualified `mcp__<server>__<tool>` form (e.g. `mcp__code_mode__call_tool_chain`), matching the `opencode.json` MCP namespace. Bare tool IDs (e.g. `advisor_recommend`) belong in instruction prose, never in `allowed-tools`.
839: 
840: **Workflow-backed families (speckit, create, deep)** additionally own `:auto` / `:confirm` workflow YAML that the router routes modes to:
841: 
842: | Asset | Owns |
843: |-------|------|
844: | `assets/<ns>-<command>-auto.yaml` | Autonomous-mode workflow: steps, agent dispatch, artifact writes. |
845: | `assets/<ns>-<command>-confirm.yaml` | Interactive-mode workflow. |
846: 
847: The **memory** and **doctor** families have NO workflow YAML. Their routers dispatch directly to tools and scripts.
848: 
849: **Canonical router shape (first-class standard).** Every router uses one canonical, numbered section vocabulary of full integers, in this order: **`## 1. ROUTER CONTRACT`**, **`## 2. OWNED ASSETS`**, **`## 3. MODE ROUTING`**, **`## 4. EXECUTION TARGETS`**, **`## 5. PRESENTATION BOUNDARY`**, **`## 6. WORKFLOW SUMMARY`**. The blocking core is only `Owned Assets` plus `Presentation Boundary`, and the other four are recommended and surface as non-blocking warnings when absent. Variants differ by hand-off only, not by required sections:
850: 
851: - **Workflow-YAML-backed** routers route modes into `-auto.yaml` / `-confirm.yaml`.
852: - **Direct-dispatch-script** routers dispatch straight to tools and scripts and may leave the recommended sections as warnings.
853: - **Compiled-stub** commands carry a `render-command-contract` marker and are exempt from section requirements (retained variant, no command currently uses it).
854: 
855: Which family uses which topology is defined by the machine-readable command contract ([`command-contract.json`](command-contract.json), validated by [`command-contract.schema.json`](command-contract.schema.json)). Read it rather than hand-maintaining a family list here.
856: 
857: Do not invent divergent synonyms (`Routing Assets`, `Workflow Routing`, `Execution Order`). The validator alias-normalizes those as a safety net, but the authored end state is the canonical names above. Reference shape: `.skilled/commands/speckit/plan.md` (router) + `speckit-plan-presentation.txt` (contract). Skeletons: [`command-router-template.md`](command-router-template.md), [`command-presentation-template.md`](command-presentation-template.md).
858: 
859: ---
860: 
861: ## 12. ARGUMENT DISPATCH PATTERN
862: 
863: Use for: Commands that accept multiple argument types and need to route to different actions.
864: 
865: ### Pattern Overview
866: 
867: When a single command handles multiple argument patterns (like `/semantic_search` accepting queries, actions, and flags), use an ASCII decision tree to document the routing logic clearly.
868: 
869: ### When to Use Argument Dispatch
870: 
871: | Scenario                                   | Use Pattern?                 |
872: | ------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------- |
873: | Command has multiple action keywords       | **Yes**                      |
874: | Command accepts both keywords AND queries  | **Yes**                      |
875: | Command has only one action                | No (use simple template)     |
876: | Command uses `:auto`/`:confirm` modes only | No (use mode-based template) |
877: 
878: ### The Pattern
879: 
880: ```markdown
881: ---
882: description: [Command] with multiple entry points
883: argument-hint: "[action|query] [options]"
884: allowed-tools: [Tools]
885: ---
886: 
887: # [Command Title]
888: 
889: ---
890: 
891: ## 1. ARGUMENT DISPATCH
892: 
893: \`\`\`
894: $ARGUMENTS
895:     │
896:     ├─► Empty (no args)
897:     │   └─► DEFAULT ACTION: [What happens with no args]
898:     │
899:     ├─► First word matches ACTION KEYWORD (case-insensitive)
900:     │   ├─► "start" | "on" | "init"       → START ACTION
901:     │   ├─► "stop" | "off" | "kill"       → STOP ACTION
902:     │   ├─► "status" | "info"             → STATUS ACTION
903:     │   ├─► "search" | "find" | "query"   → SEARCH ACTION (remaining args = query)
904:     │   └─► "reset" | "clear"             → RESET ACTION
905:     │
906:     ├─► Looks like NATURAL LANGUAGE QUERY
907:     │   Detection: 2+ words, question words, code terms, quotes
908:     │   └─► SEARCH ACTION (full args = query)
909:     │
910:     └─► Single ambiguous word
911:         └─► [DEFAULT ACTION] (assume most common intent)
912: \`\`\`
913: 
914: ---
915: 
916: ## 2. ACTION HANDLERS
917: 
918: ### START ACTION
919: [Instructions for start]
920: 
921: ### STOP ACTION
922: [Instructions for stop]
923: 
924: ### SEARCH ACTION
925: [Instructions for search]
926: 
927: ---
928: 
929: ## 3. EXAMPLE ROUTING
930: 
931: | Input                | Detected As      | Action                  |
932: | -------------------- | ---------------- | ----------------------- |
933: | (empty)              | No args          | Show menu/help          |
934: | `start`              | Keyword          | START ACTION            |
935: | `how does auth work` | Natural language | SEARCH ACTION           |
936: | `oauth`              | Single word      | SEARCH ACTION (default) |
937: ```
938: 
939: ### Real Example: `/semantic_search`
940: 
941: ```
942: /semantic_search [args]
943:     │
944:     ├─► No args
945:     │   └─► Show usage help
946:     │
947:     ├─► "index" | "reindex" | "rebuild"
948:     │   └─► INDEX ACTION: Rebuild vector index
949:     │
950:     ├─► "status" | "health"
951:     │   └─► STATUS ACTION: Show index health
952:     │
953:     ├─► Natural language query (2+ words)
954:     │   └─► SEARCH ACTION: Execute semantic search
955:     │
956:     └─► Single ambiguous word
957:         └─► SEARCH ACTION (assume search intent)
958: ```
959: 
960: ### Combining with Mode-Based Pattern
961: 
962: For commands that need BOTH argument dispatch AND mode support:
963: 
964: ```
965: $ARGUMENTS
966:     │
967:     ├─► Parse mode suffix (:auto | :confirm)
968:     │
969:     └─► After mode extraction, dispatch remaining args:
970:         ├─► "action1" → ACTION 1
971:         ├─► "action2" → ACTION 2
972:         └─► Natural language → DEFAULT ACTION
973: ```
974: 
975: ---

977: ## 13. DESTRUCTIVE COMMAND TEMPLATE
978: 
979: Use for: Commands that delete data or make irreversible changes.
980: 
981: ```markdown
982: ---
983: description: [Action] (DESTRUCTIVE)
984: argument-hint: "[--confirm]"
985: allowed-tools: Bash
986: ---
987: 
988: # [Command Title]
989: 
990: **DESTRUCTIVE OPERATION** - [Brief warning about what will be affected.]
991: 
992: ---
993: 
994: ## 1. PURPOSE
995: 
996: [Explain the destructive action and why it might be needed.]
997: 
998: ---
999: 
1000: ## 2. CONTRACT
1001: 
1002: **Inputs:** `$ARGUMENTS`, which must include the `--confirm` flag to skip the prompt
1003: **Outputs:** `STATUS=<OK|FAIL|CANCELLED> ACTION=<action|cancelled>`
1004: 
1005: ---
1006: 
1007: ## 3. INSTRUCTIONS
1008: 
1009: ### Step 1: Safety Check - Require Confirmation
1010: 
1011: - Check if `--confirm` flag is present in `$ARGUMENTS`
1012: - If NOT present:
1013:   - Ask user: "[Warning message]. Are you sure?"
1014:   - Options: "Yes, proceed" / "No, cancel"
1015:   - If user cancels: `STATUS=CANCELLED ACTION=cancelled`
1016: 
1017: ### Step 2: Show What Will Be Affected
1018: 
1019: - Display current state
1020: - List items that will be deleted/changed
1021: - Show size/count of affected data
1022: 
1023: ### Step 3: Execute Destructive Action
1024: 
1025: - [Step-by-step execution]
1026: - Log each action taken
1027: 
1028: ### Step 4: Verify Completion
1029: 
1030: - Confirm action completed
1031: - Show new state
1032: 
1033: ### Step 5: Provide Recovery Guidance
1034: 
1035: - Explain how to rebuild/restore if needed
1036: - Link to relevant commands
1037: 
1038: ### Step 6: Return Status
1039: 
1040: - If completed: `STATUS=OK ACTION=[action]`
1041: - If cancelled: `STATUS=CANCELLED ACTION=cancelled`
1042: - If failed: `STATUS=FAIL ERROR="<message>"`
1043: 
1044: ---
1045: 
1046: ## 4. EXAMPLE USAGE
1047: 
1048: ### Without Confirmation (Safe Default)
1049: 
1050: \`\`\`bash
1051: /command-name
1052: \`\`\`
1053: → Will prompt for confirmation before proceeding
1054: 
1055: ### With Confirmation Flag (Skip Prompt)
1056: 
1057: \`\`\`bash
1058: /command-name --confirm
1059: \`\`\`
1060: → Proceeds immediately (use with caution)
1061: 
1062: ---
1063: 
1064: ## 5. NOTES
1065: 
1066: - **When to Use:**
1067:   - [Valid use case 1]
1068:   - [Valid use case 2]
1069: 
1070: - **Impact:**
1071:   - [What will be lost]
1072:   - [Other consequences]
1073:   - [What is preserved]
1074:   - [Recovery options]
1075: 
1076: - **Alternatives to Consider:**
1077:   - [Less destructive alternative]
1078:   - [Another option]
1079: 
1080: ---
1081: 
1082: ## 6. SAFETY FEATURES
1083: 
1084: - Requires explicit confirmation by default
1085: - Shows what will be affected before proceeding
1086: - Provides clear recovery steps
1087: - Cannot accidentally affect [protected items]
1088: ```

1092: ## 14. NAMESPACE COMMAND PATTERN
1093: 
1094: Use for: Grouping related commands under a common prefix.
1095: 
1096: ### Directory Structure
1097: 
1098: ```
1099: .skilled/commands/
1100: └── [namespace]/           # Directory name = namespace
1101:     ├── [action1].md       # → /namespace:action1
1102:     ├── [action2].md       # → /namespace:action2
1103:     └── [action3].md       # → /namespace:action3
1104: ```
1105: 
1106: ### Example: Index Namespace
1107: 
1108: ```
1109: .skilled/commands/
1110: └── index/
1111:     ├── start.md     → /index:start
1112:     ├── stop.md      → /index:stop
1113:     ├── search.md    → /index:search
1114:     ├── stats.md     → /index:stats
1115:     ├── history.md   → /index:history
1116:     └── reset.md     → /index:reset
1117: ```
1118: 
1119: ### Naming Conventions
1120: 
1121: | Element             | Convention             | Example                      |
1122: | ------------------- | ---------------------- | ---------------------------- |
1123: | Namespace directory | lowercase, hyphen-case | `index/`, `git-workflow/`    |
1124: | Action files        | lowercase, hyphen-case | `search.md`, `full-reset.md` |
1125: | Resulting command   | namespace:action       | `/index:search`              |
1126: 
1127: Namespace and action segments must match `^[a-z0-9]+(?:-[a-z0-9]+)*$`. Reject underscore-bearing or ambiguous names, and keep each emitted `.md` stem identical to its validated action.
1128: 
1129: ---
1130: 
1131: ## 15. VALIDATION CHECKLIST
1132: 
1133: Before publishing a command, verify:
1134: 
1135: ### Frontmatter
1136: 
1137: - [ ] `description` is present and action-oriented
1138: - [ ] `argument-hint` shows expected format (if args expected)
1139: - [ ] `allowed-tools` lists all tools used (if any)
1140: - [ ] No angle brackets `< >` in description (reserved for hints)
1141: 
1142: ### Mandatory Gate (CRITICAL for required arguments)
1143: 
1144: - [ ] If `argument-hint` contains `<required>` args → **MANDATORY GATE present**
1145: - [ ] Gate sits **after the H1 and its purpose line**, before any workflow step
1146: - [ ] Gate presents options to user with appropriate question
1147: - [ ] Gate includes all 4 CRITICAL RULES (DO NOT infer, assume, proceed)
1148: - [ ] Skip gate only if ALL arguments are `[optional]` with defaults
1149: 
1150: ### Structure
1151: 
1152: - [ ] H1 title matches command purpose
1153: - [ ] H2 sections use format: `## N. SECTION-NAME` (see the Section Vocabulary)
1154: - [ ] H3 subsections: `### Step N: Description`
1155: - [ ] Dividers (`---`) between major sections
1156: - [ ] Instructions are numbered and actionable
1157: - [ ] Example usage shows 2-3 scenarios
1158: - [ ] Full integer step numbering only (no 1.5, 2.5 - see Section 5)
1159: 
1160: ### Header Format
1161: 
1162: - [ ] H1: Plain title only (`# Command Title`) or with semantic emoji for blocking sections (`# 🚨 MANDATORY PHASES`)
1163: - [ ] H2: Numbered + SECTION-NAME (`## 1. PURPOSE`)
1164: - [ ] H3/H4: Title case (`### Step 1: Description`)
1165: - [ ] Consistent numbering (1, 2, 3...)
1166: - [ ] Section names from approved vocabulary (see the Section Vocabulary)
1167: 
1168: **Blocking Phase Pattern:**
1169: Commands with mandatory input phases use these semantic markers:
1170: - `# MANDATORY PHASES` - Critical blocking section (H1)
1171: - `## PHASE N:` - Required blocking phases (H2)
1172: - `## PHASE STATUS VERIFICATION` - Gate checks (H2)
1173: - `## VIOLATION SELF-DETECTION` - Violation recovery (H2)
1174:

1177: ## 16. ORCHESTRATOR + WORKERS PATTERN
1178: 
1179: Use for: Commands that spawn parallel sub-agents for exploration/analysis.
1180: 
1181: ```
1182: OPUS ORCHESTRATOR → Dispatches → SONNET WORKERS (parallel)
1183:      │                              │
1184:      └── Synthesizes ←──────────────┘
1185: ```
1186: 
1187: | Role             | Model    | Responsibility                                        |
1188: | ---------------- | -------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
1189: | **Orchestrator** | `opus`   | Task understanding, dispatch, verification, synthesis |
1190: | **Workers**      | `sonnet` | Fast parallel exploration, hypothesis generation      |
1191: 
1192: **Use when**: Parallel codebase exploration, multi-aspect analysis, complex planning.
1193: **Skip when**: Simple single-action commands, sequential workflows.
1194:
